analysis.one_liner: Bans toxic PFAS "forever chemicals" from firefighting foam to protect firefighters.
analysis.headline: A bill to ban PFAS from firefighting foam never came up for a vote — it sat in two House committees with zero cosponsors until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal, starting two years after enactment, to make, import, process, or sell firefighting foam (known as AFFF) that contains PFAS, man-made chemicals linked to health problems. It would also require the FAA, by October 5, 2024, to prohibit fluorinated chemicals in firefighting foam at airports. PFAS exposure is a known occupational hazard for firefighters, who handle this foam in training and emergencies.
analysis.who_benefits: Firefighters, who are routinely exposed to PFAS through the foam they train and fight fires with, would see the main source of that exposure phased out of manufacture and sale, and out of airports entirely by October 2024 [S2][S3]. People living near airports and fire training grounds, where PFAS from foam has contaminated soil and water, would also benefit as the foam is pulled from the market [S2]. Violations would be enforceable under the Toxic Substances Control Act [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits, beginning two years after enactment, the manufacture, import, processing, or sale of any aqueous film forming firefighting foam (AFFF) containing PFAS, treating violations under the Toxic Substances Control Act.
Requires the FAA to prohibit fluorinated chemicals in firefighting foam at airports no later than October 5, 2024, ending a federal requirement that had pushed airports to use PFAS foam.
Targets the foam that firefighters handle repeatedly in training and emergencies; the CRS summary notes PFAS are man-made chemicals that may have adverse human health effects.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers and distributors of PFAS-containing firefighting foam would lose the product line [S2][S3]. Airports and fire departments would bear the cost of buying replacement foam and flushing equipment, and the bill contains no funding to help with that transition [S3]. Fire departments outside airports could also keep using existing stockpiles, since the bill bans making and selling the foam but not using it [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: PFAS foam makers and foam buyers

drawbacks.text: The bill bans making, importing, and selling PFAS foam but does not ban its use except at airports, so fire departments could continue using existing stockpiles after the ban takes effect.
It provides no money to help airports and fire departments replace foam and decontaminate equipment, leaving the switch costs with local budgets.

Fire services have raised good-faith questions about whether fluorine-free foams perform as well on certain fuel fires, which is why the bill ties the airport rule to the National Fire Protection Association standard rather than an immediate ban.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but focused: it removes the leading source of PFAS exposure for a specific group of workers — firefighters — and reduces contamination around airports, at the cost of lost sales for foam makers and replacement expenses for foam users with no transition funding. The design has gaps (existing stockpiles could still be used off-airport), but the core trade — a toxic exposure phased out in exchange for a manageable product switch — favors the firefighters and communities the bill was written for.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and their subcommittees and never came up for a vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Dan Kildee introduced the PFAS Firefighter Protection Act on April 27, 2022, with no cosponsors.

The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees; within a day it was sent to the Environment and Climate Change Subcommittee and the Aviation Subcommittee.
No committee or subcommittee acted on the bill, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of PFAS-containing firefighting foam kept their market, and airports kept operating under the existing fluorinated-foam requirement. Firefighters, the people the bill was written to protect, gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PFAS foam makers; firefighters gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a cosponsor from either party and never came to a vote, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.industry: PFAS chemical and firefighting foam manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would ban them from making, importing, or selling AFFF containing PFAS, eliminating their main firefighting-foam product line [S2][S3]. The same foam is the leading source of PFAS exposure for firefighters, so the industry's interest in keeping it on the market runs against the workers who use it.

Airports would have to replace fluorinated foam and certify to a new standard by October 2024, at their own expense and with no transition funding [S3]. In exchange they get relief from a federal rule that had effectively required PFAS foam on their grounds, a source of contamination and liability.
